fields.Front: Name the three levels of the three-schema architecture.
fields.Back: External level (views/external schemas), conceptual level (conceptual schema), internal level (physical schema).

fields.Text: The internal (physical) level describes the {{c1::data storage}} and the {{c2::indices}} used to get to the data.

fields.Front: What does the conceptual level describe?
fields.Back: The structure of the whole database for all users; normally the data is described as tables (the relational model).

fields.Front: What does the external level (a view) show?
fields.Back: Each view shows only the data that a particular end user is interested in and hides the other data.
The capacity to change the conceptual schema without affecting the external schemas or views.
The ability to change the physical (internal) schema without changing the conceptual schema.

fields.Text: {{c1::Logical}} data independence: change the conceptual schema without affecting the views. {{c2::Physical}} data independence: change the physical schema without changing the conceptual schema.
Adding an index changes the {{c1::internal (physical)}} level; {{c2::physical}} data independence keeps the conceptual schema (tables) unaffected.

fields.Front: Adding a column to a table changes which level, and which data independence protects existing views?
fields.Back: The conceptual level; logical data independence.

fields.Text: The goal is to have {{c1::both physical and logical}} data independence.

fields.Front: What does the instructor say lives at the internal level?
fields.Back: The hard disks, the ones and zeros that represent the data, and indices that jump quickly to a record's location on disk when a table has hundreds of thousands of records.

fields.Text: The database you build in this course is built at the {{c1::conceptual}} level (tables, columns, rows) and physically stored at the {{c2::internal}} level.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's weather-database example of two external views.
fields.Back: A web program that needs only Ontario data and a mobile app that needs all of Canada; each program is shown only the tables and data it needs.

fields.Text: Logical data independence example: adding tables for {{c1::Prince Edward Island}} to the weather database should not affect the {{c2::Ontario-only}} application; 'it shouldn't even know'.

fields.Front: What caveat does the instructor give about logical data independence?
fields.Back: If you remove a table that an application actually uses, you can break it. Independence is about changes to parts of the conceptual schema the application does not use not forcing changes to its code.

fields.Front: Give the instructor's two examples of physical data independence.
fields.Back: Moving all the data from a failing disk to a new disk; building a new index because access to tens of thousands of files is slow. Designers do not change their schema; users may only notice faster access.

fields.Front: Why does the instructor say we want both kinds of data independence?
fields.Back: It makes life easier for the DBA, designer, programmer and end user because changes at one level do not 'screw up' the other person's level.
